question: You have a Python backend service that slows down over several hours and eventually OOM crashes. How do you diagnose and fix a memory leak?
title: Diagnosing Memory Leaks in Python
direct_answer: Start with tracemalloc to identify what's growing: enable it, take snapshots before and after, and compare. Common culprits: growing collections that are never cleared (caches without eviction), circular references preventing garbage collection (though Python's cyclic GC usually handles these), event listener callbacks holding references, and global state accumulation. Use objgraph to find what object types are accumulating and where they're referenced from.
interviewer_intent: Tests real-world debugging experience — distinguishes candidates who have shipped production services from those who only know theory.

sections.title: Memory leak investigation approach
sections.content:
A slowly growing memory footprint in a long-running Python service is almost always one of three things: a collection that grows without bound (a cache, a registry, an event log that nobody clears), reference cycles that aren't being collected (less common since Python 3.4's improved cyclic GC, but possible with __del__ methods), or file descriptors / database connections that aren't being closed.

The diagnostic workflow: (1) confirm it's actually a leak, not just a legitimate load increase — memory should plateau under constant load, not grow indefinitely. (2) enable tracemalloc early — it traces allocations but has overhead, so you often need to enable it before the leak manifests. (3) take a snapshot, run load, take another snapshot, compare. tracemalloc.take_snapshot() and compare_to() shows you which lines of code allocated the most memory. (4) use objgraph.show_growth() to see which object types are accumulating. objgraph.show_backrefs(objects) shows what's holding references.

Common fixes: add a maxsize to caches (functools.lru_cache(maxsize=1000) or cachetools.TTLCache), use weakref.WeakValueDictionary or WeakSet for registries where the registry shouldn't own the objects, ensure database connections go through a context manager, audit any global lists or dicts that accumulate records.

sections.title: Diagnostic tooling
sections.content:
import tracemalloc
import linecache

# Enable early (in startup code, not at leak site)
tracemalloc.start()

# ... run the server for a while ...

# Take a snapshot and report top allocations
snapshot = tracemalloc.take_snapshot()
top_stats = snapshot.statistics('lineno')
for stat in top_stats[:10]:
    print(stat)

# Compare two snapshots to see what grew
snap1 = tracemalloc.take_snapshot()
# ... handle requests ...
snap2 = tracemalloc.take_snapshot()
stats = snap2.compare_to(snap1, 'lineno')
for stat in stats[:10]:
    print(stat)

# objgraph for object counts (pip install objgraph)
import objgraph
objgraph.show_growth(limit=10)  # top growing types

# Common fix: bounded cache
from functools import lru_cache
@lru_cache(maxsize=512)          # bounded — evicts LRU entries
def expensive_lookup(key: str) -> dict:
    return db.fetch(key)

# Common fix: TTL cache
from cachetools import TTLCache
cache = TTLCache(maxsize=1000, ttl=300)  # evicts after 5 minutes

# Weak reference registry — doesn't prevent GC
import weakref
class EventBus:
    def __init__(self):
        self._listeners = weakref.WeakSet()  # GC'd when listener is deleted

    def subscribe(self, listener):
        self._listeners.add(listener)

sections.title: Traps that cause subtle leaks
sections.content: Closures capturing large objects: a background thread whose target function closes over a large DataFrame keeps that DataFrame alive until the thread finishes. Mutable default arguments that grow: def append_to(item, to=[]): to.append(item) — the list accumulates across calls. SQLAlchemy sessions left open: unpurged in-memory unit-of-work state. Django's translation cache growing indefinitely for unique-per-request strings. FastAPI route parameters captured in background tasks.

sections.title: Memory leak investigation checklist
items: tracemalloc: enable at startup, compare snapshots after load
objgraph.show_growth(): finds which types are accumulating
Top suspects: unbounded dicts/lists, global registries, thread locals
Caches: always set maxsize or TTL — functools.lru_cache(maxsize=N)
Connections: always use context managers or connection pools
weakref.WeakValueDictionary for registries that shouldn't own objects

items: Unbounded caches — no maxsize, grows forever
Global lists or dicts accumulating records each request
Event listeners holding references to objects that should be GC'd
Database connections not closed, keeping result sets in memory

speakable_v2.cap: The most common fix I've seen: someone added an in-memory dict as a 'temporary cache' without a TTL, and it grew for years. Always set maxsize and TTL on caches.

question: How do you resolve circular import errors in Python?
title: Circular Imports in Python
direct_answer: Circular imports happen when module A imports B, and B imports A. Python partially initializes modules, so when A tries to import B while B is still loading A, it gets an incomplete module. The fixes: move the import inside the function (local import), restructure to extract shared code into a third module that neither A nor B imports from the other, or use TYPE_CHECKING guard for type hints that only matter at type-check time, not runtime.
interviewer_intent: Tests understanding of Python's import system and the ability to recognize and resolve a common architecture smell in medium-to-large codebases.

sections.title: Why circular imports happen and how Python handles them
sections.content:
Python executes module code top-to-bottom when first imported and caches the result in sys.modules. When module A is imported, Python starts executing it. If A imports B, and B imports A, Python finds A already in sys.modules but only partially initialized — the attributes defined before the import statement are there, but later ones aren't. This is why you often see 'cannot import name X from partially initialized module Y'.

The three structural solutions:

1. Local imports: move the import inside the function that uses it. The import only happens when the function is called, by which time both modules are fully loaded. Downside: it's a code smell that signals a layering violation — use sparingly and leave a comment.

2. Refactor: extract the shared dependency into a third module. If models.py imports utils.py for validation, and utils.py imports models.py for type hints, create a types.py or schemas.py that holds the types, and have both import from there.

3. TYPE_CHECKING guard: from __future__ import annotations plus TYPE_CHECKING lets you write type annotations that reference other modules without triggering a real import at runtime. The import only runs when a type checker analyzes the code.

Circular imports are almost always a sign of poor layering. The real fix is to redraw the dependency graph so it's a DAG (no cycles).

sections.title: Resolving circular imports
sections.content:
# Problem: models.py and services.py import each other
# models.py
from services import UserService   # causes circular import

class User:
    def activate(self):
        UserService.send_welcome_email(self)

# Fix 1: local import
class User:
    def activate(self):
        from services import UserService   # import at call time
        UserService.send_welcome_email(self)

# Fix 2: extract shared types to types.py
# types.py
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class UserDTO:
    id: int
    email: str

# models.py — imports only from types.py
from types_module import UserDTO

# services.py — imports only from types.py
from types_module import UserDTO

# Fix 3: TYPE_CHECKING guard (for type hints only)
from __future__ import annotations
from typing import TYPE_CHECKING

if TYPE_CHECKING:
    from services import UserService   # only runs during mypy/pyright, not at runtime

class User:
    def get_service(self) -> 'UserService':   # quote or use annotations import
        ...

sections.title: Circular import strategies
items: Local import (inside function) fixes the runtime error but is a smell
TYPE_CHECKING guard: safe for type hints, doesn't import at runtime
Refactor to a shared module — the real architectural fix
Circular imports signal a layering violation in the module graph
Check sys.modules to see which modules are partially loaded

speakable_v2.hook: Circular imports aren't a Python bug — they're Python telling you that your module dependency graph has a cycle that needs untangling.

beats.content: Python executes module code top-to-bottom and caches in sys.modules. When A imports B and B imports A, Python hands B a partially-initialized A — attributes defined before the import are there, later ones aren't. That's the AttributeError or ImportError you see.

items: Local import inside the function — quick fix, but marks an architectural smell
TYPE_CHECKING guard — for type hints only, zero runtime cost
Extract shared types to a third module — the real structural fix

beats.content: Every circular import is a signal: two modules are too tightly coupled. The lasting fix is to draw your dependency graph as a DAG — models depends on types, services depends on models, routes depend on services.

speakable_v2.cap: If you're adding a local import to fix a circular dependency, add a comment explaining why — and add a ticket to fix the architecture properly.
